title: What are the chances a flag caught abuse?

beats.say: In this example, each filled circle marks a signup the detector flagged. We start with a hundred signups already known to be abusive. The punch caught ninety-five. Can you find the five it missed?
Tear off the flagged part and keep it. If a reviewer picks one flag at random from the whole queue, would you expect most of those flags to have caught abuse?

Keep those ninety-five. Now feed in the flags from clean signups. There are four hundred ninety-five of them. Lay the two strips end to end. About one flag in six caught abuse. Where did that long blue strip come from?

title: Who could we have picked?

beats.say: Put the hundred abusive signups in one red bundle. Bring in the clean signups from the same labeled batch. Each blue bundle holds another hundred. Pick one signup uniformly from all ten thousand. That means every signup has the same chance. All the signups we could pick form our sample space.
An event is a subset of the possible picks. For the event called abuse, keep just the signups in the red bundle.

One red bundle out of a hundred gives one percent. That's the prior, the chance of abuse before seeing a flag. To estimate it for tomorrow, sample incoming signups whether the detector flags them or lets them through.

title: What does one randomly picked label look like?

beats.say: Write one on each abusive signup and zero on each clean one. The number you get depends on which signup you pick. That's a random variable. For a zero-or-one label like this, the name is Bernoulli. Multiply each value by its population share, then add.
That average is the expected value. Here it's the same one percent we got by counting.

One actual pick still gives zero or one. Variance averages squared distances from the mean. A one lies almost a whole unit away, but it turns up only one time in a hundred. The zeros crowd right up against the mean.

Weight each square by how often its label occurs. Add the two pieces and the variance is point zero zero nine nine. For any Bernoulli label with chance p of a one, the variance is p times one minus p. Later we'll measure the spread of a rate estimated from many labels.

title: Let each source send its flags

beats.say: The detector flags ninety-five percent inside the abusive source and five percent inside the clean source. Keep those denominators separate. A small rate on a large source can contribute the larger pile. Before the pieces arrive, predict which color will dominate review.

Follow the abusive flags onto the roll. The first source supplies ninety-five tickets. Now feed in the clean flags. That source supplies four hundred ninety-five. The length of each color counts signups on the same scale. The roll keeps both groups in the order they arrived.

Now count everyone in the queue. Ninety-five plus four hundred ninety-five gives five hundred ninety reviews. The blue packets dominate. Recall counted inside abuse. The reviewer is about to divide inside a different population.

title: Keep the intersection, change the world

beats.say: Here's the whole batch sorted by what the detector did. Five abusive signups went through with the clean ones. Slide a window over just the flagged column. The ninety-five abusive flags stay under the window. If we pick a signup from this window, what goes in the denominator?

Divide the ninety-five abusive flags by all five hundred ninety selected signups. The result is about sixteen percent. That's the risk for the signup on your desk after seeing its flag. We call it the posterior. Read the vertical bar as given.
The right side tells you which signups go in the window. The left side tells you what to count among them.

Turn the window the other way. Given abuse, how often was there a flag? The window now includes the five misses and leaves out the clean signups. The same ninety-five abusive flags sit inside one hundred abusive signups. That fraction is ninety-five percent.

title: Give the counting a compact name

beats.say: Pick from all ten thousand again. Count both events together, abusive and flagged. That joint event has ninety-five rows out of ten thousand. Add flags from both sources for the marginal flag probability. Conditional probability divides the joint share by the selected world's share. The common population scale cancels.

Build the joint share another way: abuse prior times the flag rate within abuse. Replace the joint term with that product and we have Bayes' rule. Its denominator includes every way a flag can arise. These symbols preserve the counting we already checked.

title: Same detector, different traffic

beats.say: The flag on our desk came from a batch with one percent abuse. Suppose another signup surface has ten percent abuse in a batch of the same size. Keep both detector rates fixed. First predict the direction of queue risk. Would you expect a larger or a smaller fraction of the queue to be abusive?

Change the prior and follow both contributions. The red part grows to nine hundred fifty flags. The blue part actually shrinks. Five percent now applies to fewer clean signups. How much of the queue is red?

Nine hundred fifty out of fourteen hundred gives about sixty-eight percent. Same behavior within each class, very different odds on the reviewer's desk. On real traffic we'd check all three rates again.

title: What would equal selection rates do?

beats.say: Return to the one-percent population and try a different detector. It flags twenty percent of each class. Should its flag change our abuse probability? Both classes pass through the same fraction. Predict the composition before we join the selected pieces.

Tear one fifth from each source and join the selected pieces. Twenty abusive signups sit beside nineteen hundred eighty clean signups. That's twenty out of two thousand flags, still one percent abusive. When knowing one event happened leaves the probability of the other unchanged, the events are independent. This detector creates review work while preserving the original mix.

Independence differs from mutual exclusion. Abuse and clean cannot both describe the same binary label. Learning abuse makes clean impossible, changing its probability from ninety-nine percent to zero, so those two events are not independent.

title: Does a copied flag narrow the queue?

beats.say: The review queue has five hundred ninety signups. A second service copies every flag. If a reviewer keeps only signups with both flags, which signups drop out?

Look at the serial numbers on the two tickets. They match because the second field copies the first. Keeping both flags keeps all five hundred ninety signups. The abuse fraction stays at sixteen percent.

Now give each detector its own test. Keep the original flag rates. If the tests are independent within each class, multiply the two rates for that class. Among clean signups, the first test flags five percent. The second flags five percent of those.

That leaves about twenty-five clean signups on average. Nearly four fifths of the signups with both flags are abusive. When detectors share rules, count how often they both flag the same signup in each class.

title: When can the function return a risk?

beats.say: Turn the count into a function. Give it the original one-percent prior and the two flag rates. Each input must be a finite number between zero and one. A prior of one point four is an error.

The red contribution is the prior times recall, the fraction caught among abusive signups. Add the false-flag mass from the remaining population. Dividing the red part by the whole strip recovers the risk we counted.
Turn both flag rates down to zero. The prior stays at one percent. How much can each source contribute, and who could be in the review queue?

Abusive signups contribute zero. Clean signups also contribute zero. Add the two sources and the denominator is zero. The conditional fraction is zero divided by zero. That probability is undefined. Report the empty event to the caller.

Now try a numerical stress test. Call the smallest positive number a sixty-four-bit float can store one unit. Set the prior and the clean flag rate to one unit each. Recall is one half. The abusive flag mass lands halfway between zero and one unit.
At that tie the product rounds down to zero. The clean mass rounds to one unit. Direct division reports zero risk. Both sources could actually produce a flag.

Go back to the inputs, while they're still positive. For each group, add the log of its population share to the log of its flag rate. That gives the two log masses. The difference between them survives even at this tiny scale.

Subtract the larger log mass from both and exponentiate. This is the scaling step in log-sum-exp. On that common scale, the red contribution is about half the blue one. Red gets about a third of the queue. A tiny event can have a perfectly ordinary conditional probability.

title: Freeze the labels, move the candidate rate

beats.say: What if the queue's abuse rate is unknown? Take three reviewed outcomes in this order, abuse, clean, abuse. Keep those labels fixed. Try a candidate rate called p. Assume the labels are independent draws at that rate. Each abuse contributes p. The clean label contributes one minus p. Multiply the three assigned probabilities.

At a candidate rate of one fifth, this sequence is fairly unlikely. Move the candidate to four fifths and recompute each factor. The labels stay still while their assigned probabilities change. The product increases. This comparison of candidate explanations is a likelihood.

Follow the point on the likelihood curve. Its peak sits at two abuses out of three. Its height is the probability of those three labels in that order if the rate is two thirds. In Bayesian inference we combine this likelihood with a prior over rates.

Try a prior that gives equal weight to just two candidate rates, one fifth and four fifths. Multiply each prior weight by the likelihood of the observed sequence, then normalize the weights to sum to one. The four-fifths candidate now has four times as much posterior weight as the one-fifth candidate.

If we observe only two abuses out of three and discard their order, three sequences qualify. The count probability is three times the ordered-sequence likelihood. That factor changes the probability of the observed event, while the maximizing rate remains two thirds.

title: Would you quote this score as a risk?

beats.say: A reviewer opens six signups scored close to point eight. If those scores are good probabilities, we'd expect abuse about eight times in ten across a large group like this. Uncover the six labels. What fraction in this little group is actually abusive?

Three divided by six is point five. Mark that on the same ruler as the average score. The gap here is thirty percentage points. Checking observed frequencies against predictions in groups like this is called calibration.

Six labels give us one noisy comparison. To use scores on all incoming signups, check representative cases across score ranges, including signups the detector let through. Now give every signup in the original batch a score of one percent. A hundred of the ten thousand were abusive. Which of these two signups should the score send to review first?
The two scores tie. The one-percent forecast matches the observed frequency across this batch, but it gives the reviewer no way to put one signup ahead of the other.

title: What values can we observe?

beats.say: Take ten independent signups, each with a one percent chance of abuse. Each label is Bernoulli, zero or one. Add the ten labels. That's a binomial count. This batch has one abusive signup. What count would we expect on average across many batches?

Each signup contributes one hundredth to the expected count. Slide those ten pieces together. That's a tenth per batch, or one abusive signup per ten batches on average. With n signups at probability p, the mean count is n times p. Independent labels let us add their variances too, giving n times p times one minus p.

Now count alerts in a minute. There's no fixed number of trials. If alerts arrive independently at a steady rate of two per minute, a Poisson model gives the count both a mean and a variance of two. Even a quiet minute with no alerts is possible.

Its zero-count probability is e to minus two. For a continuous measurement like a timing error, a Normal model may be more reasonable. Match the possible values and the assumptions to what you're measuring. On a continuous curve, the area over an interval gives the probability of landing in that range.

title: Which token comes next?

beats.say: Try finishing the words 'function returns the'. In this little model there are four possible next tokens. Look at banana. Its score is below zero. These raw scores are called logits. Exponentiate each score and divide by the shared sum.
Each token now owns a positive share of one strip. This is a categorical distribution, and the operation that built it is called softmax.

Watch the widths. Subtract the largest logit before exponentiating. Every weight gets divided by the same factor, so their shares stay put. Now even the largest exponential is only one, which avoids overflow. The gap of point eight between result and value is still there.
That makes result about two point two three times as likely as value.

Greedy decoding takes the widest segment, result, every time we repeat this exact request. To sample, pick a point uniformly along the strip. Our first point lands on result. Here the sample and the greedy choice agree. Make another draw on the very same strip. This one lands on None. Both draws used exactly the same token probabilities.

Keep drawing from that same distribution. The repeated draws fluctuate around its probabilities. In a thousand draws we'd expect about six hundred eighteen copies of result. A fixed seed lets us replay this particular sample. Another seed can give us a different count.

title: What chance did the model give this line?

beats.say: Now score a line someone actually wrote. In our toy vocabulary, each word in 'rain fell here' is one token. The first probability belongs to rain at the start. The second belongs to fell after rain. The third belongs to here after both words.
For three supplied probabilities point five, point two and point one, what probability did the model give the whole line?

It is point zero one. Multiply the three factors. That's the chain rule. Each probability already accounts for the prefix at that position, so this multiplication even works when earlier words strongly influence later ones.

A much longer line can break that calculation on a computer. Give each of two hundred tokens the same probability of one hundredth. Follow the sum of logs as the sequence grows. The mathematical product is ten to the minus four hundred.

A sixty-four-bit float stores that product as zero, but the natural logs still add up to about minus nine hundred twenty-one. Keep that finite log probability. A genuinely impossible token would have log probability minus infinity.

Back to our three words. Take the negative natural log of each target probability. We measure those losses in nats. Add them and divide by the three tokens we scored. That's about one point five three five nats per token.

Exponentiate the average and you get a perplexity of about four point six four. To compare models this way, use comparable data, tokenization and scoring masks. The model is scoring the words someone wrote. Their probability tells us little about whether it actually rained.

title: How much does the fourth token cost?

beats.say: Find the probability assigned to the token that actually occurred, then take its negative natural log. That's cross-entropy for one observed target. A target probability point nine costs about point one zero five nats. At point zero one it costs about four point six zero five. As target probability approaches zero, this penalty grows without bound.

Give three models the same four targets. The moderate model has a mean loss of point six one nine nats. The unsure model gives every target one chance in four, for a mean of one point three eight six. The confident model gives the first three targets point nine nine each. For the fourth it gives just point zero zero one. What does that fourth token cost? Where will this model's mean fall?

Take the negative natural log of one thousandth. That fourth bar reaches six point nine zero eight nats. Each of the first three costs about point zero one zero nats. Add the four losses and divide by four. The mean comes to one point seven three four nats per token, the highest of the three models on this text.

Four observed tokens let us compare losses on this text. To check calibration we'd need many outcomes in each score range. Look what happens if we feed these probabilities to a loss function that expects logits. PyTorch CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits. It normalizes them internally.
Normalizing an extra time changes the target's share and the loss even though we're still scoring the same token. Also check which tokens enter the average.

title: The rate changes even when the system does not

beats.say: Imagine grading one unchanged system over and over on fresh sets of fifty cases. Each dot marks one test's pass rate. A reported pass rate needs a sample size because the cases you happen to draw can move the dot.

Assume independent cases with the same chance of passing. The pass count has binomial variance, n times p times one minus p. Dividing the count by n divides its variance by n squared. The square root is the standard error of the rate.

At p point eight and fifty cases, that standard error is about point zero five seven. A band extending two standard errors either way reaches about eleven percentage points below and above eighty percent. That's how much repeated tests can fluctuate under this model.
In practice we often plug in the observed pass rate. For small samples or very rare failures, use an interval suited to binomial counts. For related cases, account for their groups.

Quadrupling the number of independent cases halves this standard error. More labels from a biased flagged queue still do not estimate the all-signup prior. Sampling noise, population selection and distribution shift are separate questions.

title: The comparison has its own sampling noise

beats.say: On separate sets of fifty independent cases, the new model passes forty-two and the old model passes forty. Would you ship on that four-point lead? Think about where the gap might land on a fresh pair of tests.

To find the noise in their difference, add their rate variances and take the square root. One standard error of the gap is nearly eight percentage points. A rough two-standard-error margin is about fifteen points. This test leaves the direction of the advantage open.

What if both models take the very same test? Stack their marks in pairs, one pair per case. Suppose both pass thirty-nine, only the new model passes three, only the old model passes one, and both fail seven. Set aside the pairs that agree.

Three cases swing the score toward the new model. One swings it back. That's the entire four-point gap. For a paired comparison, estimate uncertainty from these case-by-case differences, keeping related cases grouped.

For rough planning near eighty percent on independent samples, making two standard errors as small as a two-point gap takes about three thousand two hundred cases per model. To clear that threshold reliably under a true two-point advantage needs more cases and a chosen power target.
Halving the target gap roughly quadruples the required count. A paired design can help when models make correlated errors.

title: Which threshold can the team staff?

beats.say: Back at the signup desk, the team has two hundred review slots. Broad review sends five hundred ninety signups from our labeled batch. Raise the score needed to qualify for review. Follow the blue strip as three hundred ninety-six clean signups leave the queue.
Watch the red strip too. Fifteen abusive signups lose their tickets. In this batch their IDs run from A eighty-one through A ninety-five. They join the five we already missed.

The strict queue now holds one hundred seventy-nine signups. Eighty are abusive. That share of the queue, about forty-five percent, is the detector's precision. Which queue fits two hundred review slots? Before you pick, count how many abusive signups will never reach a reviewer.

The strict queue fits. With these two settings, that choice leaves twenty abusive signups outside review. If the cost of those misses is too high, the team needs more slots or a detector that sends a different mix.

title: One more detector for the original batch

beats.say: Keep the same labeled batch of one hundred abusive and ninety-nine hundred clean signups. Suppose a new detector flags ninety-five percent of abusive signups and one percent of clean signups. Compared with strict review, how many more abusive signups does it catch overall? How many tickets will the team need to review?

Look at one possible set of matched records. Suppose the new detector keeps all eighty abusive signups that strict review caught. Bring back the fifteen tickets from A eighty-one through A ninety-five. That gives ninety-five catches, fifteen more overall. One percent of ninety-nine hundred clean signups still gives ninety-nine clean flags.

Ninety-five plus ninety-nine gives one hundred ninety-four reviews and leaves five abusive signups outside review. Six slots are still free. Other sets of flagged signups could give those same counts. Our opening flag meant about sixteen-percent risk because we counted every source. Rebuild the selected population whenever the evidence or the population changes.

title: Would you staff this queue?

beats.say: You're staffing review for twenty thousand incoming signups. You have nine hundred slots. Suppose three percent of signups are abusive. The detector flags eighty percent of abusive signups and two percent of clean ones. Does the expected queue fit? How many abusive signups would you miss?

Split the batch first. The prior gives six hundred abusive signups and nineteen thousand four hundred clean. Take eighty percent from the red group. That's four hundred eighty true flags. Take two percent from the much bigger blue group. That's three hundred eighty-eight false flags.

Together that's eight hundred sixty-eight expected reviews. There's room for thirty-two more. Six hundred were abusive to begin with. That leaves one hundred twenty abusive signups outside review on average. For a reviewer opening a flag, four hundred eighty out of eight hundred sixty-eight gives a risk of about fifty-five percent.

Keep the batch, the recall and the staffing exactly as they were. Change just the clean flag rate from two to two and a half percent. You've got those thirty-two empty slots. Will the extra flags fit?

Apply that extra half percentage point to the clean signups. That's ninety-seven more tickets for the reviewers. Thirty-two fit in the empty slots. The other sixty-five cross the staffing line. Look where the blue strip ends.

Both settings catch four hundred eighty abusive signups on average. The extra work comes from clean signups. Sixty-five more slots would cover the second queue's expected workload. Actual arrivals can vary. Budget a margin if the team needs to clear the queue on busy days too. Next, Bayesian inference uses new observations to update which underlying rates you consider plausible.
